You'd never expect a golden orb on the seafloor.
But in 2023, NOAA found one, two miles deep. What was it, actually?
That's the first of six strange things found in the deep sea.
For each one, we'll look at what was actually found, and give an honest verdict: solved, best guess, or still unknown.
Number one: the golden orb.
On the thirtieth of August, 2023, NOAA's ship Okeanos Explorer was exploring a small underwater mountain in the Gulf of Alaska, using a remotely operated robot.
About 3,300 meters down, on a rocky ledge among white sponges, the cameras found something nobody expected.
A smooth, gold, dome-shaped object, a little over 10 centimeters across, stuck tightly to the rock. It had a small hole near its base, and the inside was the same golden color.
One videographer on board first called it a yellow hat.
Scientists watching live were stumped. Was it a dead sponge? Coral? An egg case?
The internet called it the golden orb, or even the golden egg.
The robot sucked it up with a sampling tube and brought it to the ship. But even there, the team could only say one thing for sure: it was biological.
The expedition coordinator said: it serves as a reminder of how little we know about our own planet.
The orb was sent to NOAA Fisheries' National Systematics Laboratory, at the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History in Washington.
Scientists looked at its cells under the microscope, and read its DNA.
They found special stinging cells called spirocysts, which only one group of animals has.
And the DNA was almost identical to a known species.
That species had been seen alive before. In 2016, an Okeanos Explorer expedition near the Mariana Islands photographed a live one.
And in April 2026, about two and a half years after it was found, NOAA announced the answer.
The orb was once part of the base of a giant deep-sea anemone, a species called Relicanthus daphneae. The part that holds the animal to the rock.
Not an egg. Not an alien. Just the leftover foot of a sea anemone.
Verdict: solved. It was part of a deep-sea anemone.
Number two: the holes in the seafloor.
In 2022, NOAA explored the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, a huge underwater mountain range running down the middle of the Atlantic Ocean.
On three separate dives, the robot's cameras showed something strange in the sediment.
Lines of holes. Dozens of them, in fairly straight rows, across an otherwise flat, sandy seafloor.
The first set was about 2,540 meters deep.
NOAA's own words: the holes look almost human made.
But the little piles of sediment around them suggest something dug them out.
These holes aren't new. Similar holes had been reported from the region before, as far back as 2004.
No one has seen what makes them. The robot couldn't peek inside or poke them. On a later dive, it sucked up sediment from fresher holes. It gave no clues.
Scientists who studied the earlier holes think an animal may have dug them, either living in the sediment, or feeding from the surface. They call them life traces.
Is it an animal burrowing? Something feeding as it moves? Nobody knows.
Verdict: still unknown. Something digs them. We just haven't caught it.
Number three: the real kraken.
For centuries, sailors told stories about giant sea monsters with long arms.
In Norse legend, the kraken was a tentacled monster as large as an island, able to drag ships under.
The legend may have grown from a real animal: the giant squid.
Giant squid can reach around twelve meters long, counting their long feeding tentacles. And they have the largest eyes of almost any living animal, up to at least 27 centimeters across.
For a long time, scientists only knew them from dead bodies washed up on beaches or caught in nets.
Then, in 2004, a Japanese team led by Tsunemi Kubodera lowered a baited camera deep into the Pacific. And for the first time, they photographed a live giant squid in its natural home.
In July 2012, a team finally filmed one alive in the deep, swimming in the dark.
The monster turned out to be real. Just not as large as an island.
Verdict: solved. The kraken was probably the giant squid, a real animal.
Number four: the milky seas.
For hundreds of years, sailors described something eerie. At night, the sea around their ship would glow, a steady pale light stretching to the horizon.
Jules Verne even wrote about it. In Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas, his ship sails through a sea of milk.
Between 1915 and 1993, there were 235 recorded sightings, many of them in the northwestern Indian Ocean.
But nobody could study it properly. You can't plan to be in the right place on the right night.
In 1985, a research ship got lucky. It sailed into a milky sea in the Arabian Sea, took water samples, and found glowing bacteria.
Then scientists found a new way to look: from space.
In 2005, Steven Miller and his team matched satellite images from 1995 with a ship's report. The glowing patch was about 15,400 square kilometers, roughly the size of Connecticut.
Newer satellites have since spotted more events, including one huge glow south of Java in 2009.
Miller's team found a dozen milky seas between 2012 and 2021. But satellites can only see them on dark nights, because moonlight is hundreds of times brighter than the glow.
The leading explanation is bacteria. When enough of them gather together, they all switch on their light at once. One idea is that they're feeding on a bloom of algae.
But that 1985 voyage is still the only time scientists have sampled a milky sea up close.
Verdict: best guess. Probably glowing bacteria, but we've barely seen it up close.
Number five: dark oxygen.
On Earth, almost all oxygen comes from living things that use sunlight, like plants and algae.
So in 2024, a study in the journal Nature Geoscience made a stunning claim.
On the deep seafloor between Mexico and Hawaii, there are metal lumps the size of potatoes, called nodules.
The team measured oxygen in sealed chambers on the seafloor. Instead of going down, it went up.
Over two days, it rose to more than three times the starting level.
They suggested the metal nodules act a bit like batteries, splitting seawater to make oxygen in total darkness. They called it dark oxygen.
If it's true, it would change our understanding of where oxygen comes from.
But other scientists pushed back hard. In December 2025, critics argued in another journal that the idea is fundamentally at odds with thermodynamics.
They suggested the oxygen might have come from air trapped inside the measuring equipment.
The original team says they have more than enough evidence, and they plan to send robots back to the seafloor to check.
This matters beyond science. Companies want to mine those same nodules for their metals.
Verdict: still unknown. The claim is disputed, and new measurements are on the way.
Number six: the giants of the deep.
In the deep sea, many animals grow much larger than their relatives in shallow water.
There are giant isopods, relatives of the little pill bugs in your garden, but far bigger.
There's the giant phantom jelly, the giant sea spider, and squid like the colossal squid, which can reach around fourteen meters.
Scientists call this deep-sea gigantism. But why does it happen?
There are several ideas. Cold water slows animals down, and cold-water animals tend to grow bigger and live longer.
Colder temperatures may lead to bigger cells and longer lives, and both can add up to a larger body.
Food is scarce in the deep, and bigger bodies can travel farther and survive longer between meals.
There may be fewer predators. And cold water can hold more oxygen, which large bodies need.
The problem is the deep sea is very hard to study. Most of it has never been seen at all.
Verdict: best guess. Several good ideas, but no single answer.
So, let's check the scoreboard.
The golden orb: solved. Part of a deep-sea anemone.
The holes in the seafloor: still unknown.
The kraken: solved. The giant squid.
The milky seas: best guess. Glowing bacteria.
Dark oxygen: still unknown.
The giants of the deep: best guess.
Two solved, two best guesses, and two we still can't explain. Most of the deep sea has never been seen, and it still has plenty of secrets.
